lesson.title: Filling the Factories the Men Left Behind
lesson.summary: As millions of men left for military service, American women moved into war industry jobs in unprecedented numbers, reshaping ideas about what work women could do.
lesson.body:
The home front war production effort described in the previous chapter needed workers, and by 1943 the country was running out of men to supply them. Over sixteen million Americans eventually served in the armed forces during the war, pulling a huge share of the male workforce out of factories, shipyards, and offices at the very moment war industry needed more hands than ever. The government and private employers turned, often reluctantly at first, to a labor pool that had long been steered toward domestic work or a narrow range of 'acceptable' jobs: American women.

Millions of women took jobs in shipyards, aircraft plants, munitions factories, and steel mills, doing work that had almost always been reserved for men, including welding, riveting, and operating heavy machinery. The share of American women in the paid workforce rose substantially during the war, and government propaganda campaigns actively encouraged the shift, framing factory work as a patriotic duty rather than a break from tradition. Women also served in uniform in noncombat roles: the Women's Army Corps, the Navy's WAVES, and the Women Airforce Service Pilots, who ferried military aircraft across the country and freed male pilots for combat duty, though WASP pilots served without full military status at the time.

This wartime shift did not appear out of nowhere. It rested on decades of women's political organizing, most visibly the campaign that had won the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920 and secured women's right to vote. That earlier movement had established women as full political citizens; the war years extended the argument for full participation into the economic sphere, even if only as an emergency measure in most employers' eyes.

The shift proved only partly permanent. When the war ended and millions of servicemen returned looking for jobs, many women were laid off or pressured to leave factory work and return to domestic roles, and postwar culture pushed hard to reestablish prewar norms about women's place. Still, the experience of earning wages, learning trades, and working outside the home stayed with a generation of women, and it planted an idea that proved difficult to fully undo: that women could do the same skilled industrial work as men when given the chance. That idea would resurface with force in the women's movements of later decades.
